title: The Cult of Rigor
author: Patrick Dempsey
summary: Dempsey responds to educators who defended high-stress assessments such as the Blue Book as character building. He argues that this belief confuses hazing with education: the exam serves the instructor's wish to see students struggle, not the student's learning. Using a golf-coach analogy, he contrasts a coach who says get ready, one who assigns volume, and one who diagnoses weaknesses, assigns targeted drills and gives feedback. His claim is that a course should be the practice facility, not the tournament, and that deliberate practice with feedback, not stress and ambiguity, builds competence. He frames the shift as moving from judge to coach and says that if endurance or ambiguity tolerance are goals, they should be named and taught directly. He also notes that arbitrary assignments push students toward ChatGPT as the rational shortcut.
points: Stress-based assessment is defended as resilience training, but Dempsey says its real function is letting the instructor watch students struggle.
The coach-versus-judge distinction recasts assessment as improving performance during the process, not evaluating it afterward.
Deliberate practice, protected conditions, reflection and informative feedback are what build skill; ambiguity, time pressure and high stakes are impediments.
If a teacher wants students to develop endurance or handle ambiguity, those goals must be named and explicitly designed for.
Disconnected, arbitrary assignments invite students to game the system, increasingly via ChatGPT.
quotes: When I posted a satirical take on Pedagogical Regression™, I expected pushback. What I didn't expect was how many educators would rally to defend the Blue Book like it was a very part of their teaching soul.
Then comes test day. Showtime. The moment students “get to prove” their preparation in your format, your medium, your timeframe.
Research shows that “a sufficient amount of experience or practice doesn't lead to maximal performance.” Not even close.

The truth is simpler: your course should be the practice facility. The place where students develop skills they'll need to excel when it actually matters. Where they can fail safely, get feedback quickly, and improve systematically.
Your Blue Book turns you into a judge. You sit back, watch students struggle, then render your verdict on their performance.

You don’t prepare for the next golf tournament by playing in the next golf tournament. You prepare by working on the specific skills you need to get better so that you can be more prepared for the next golf tournament!
